summary: This informational document states the problem of localized routing in Proxy Mobile IPv6. Normally all traffic goes through the Local Mobility Anchor, even between two nearby nodes. It describes why and where direct paths between access gateways would help.

plainLanguage.summary: Two neighbors' letters travel through a faraway post office. This notes the waste and asks for a direct path.

questions: route optimization in proxy mobile ipv6
subtitle: Routing data directly between access gateways instead of through a distant anchor.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 anchors all mobile node traffic at a Local Mobility Anchor, so packets between two nearby nodes traverse the core network unnecessarily. This wastes bandwidth and introduces latency.
tldr.mechanism: The network infrastructure detects when two mobile nodes can communicate directly and sets up localized routing states on their access gateways to forward data without involving the Mobility Anchor.
tldr.outcome: Direct paths reduce core network load, lower latency, and improve scalability by offloading the LMA. The challenge is coordinating this signaling across multiple gateways and handling mobility events correctly.

facts.label: Default traffic path
facts.value: All packets through Local Mobility Anchor

facts.label: Localized routing benefit
facts.value: Direct forwarding between access gateways without LMA

today: RFC 6279 is an Informational RFC identifying the problem space for localized routing in PMIPv6. It has not been obsoleted and serves as the basis for protocol solutions (such as those in RFC 6705 and related extensions) to enable localized routing in mobile networks.

sections.title: The PMIPv6 Problem
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) is the IETF Standard for network-based mobility management. Mobile nodes are anchored at a Local Mobility Anchor (LMA), which forwards all data for registered mobile nodes.

The problem: when two mobile nodes communicate with each other, their data always traverses the LMA, even if both nodes are attached to the same access gateway or to different gateways in the same local domain. This creates unnecessary load on the LMA and introduces latency.

Localized routing allows direct forwarding between two nodes' Mobility Access Gateways (MAGs) without LMA involvement. This document describes the problem space and requirements for implementing localized routing in PMIPv6 networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The postal service sends a letter from kid A to kid B through the main office 100 miles away, even though they live next door. It works, but it is slow and expensive.

sections.title: Why Localized Routing Matters
sections.content:
In Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6), mobile nodes can signal for route optimization directly. In PMIPv6, mobile nodes are not involved in mobility signaling, so they cannot request direct routes themselves. Instead, the network infrastructure must detect the opportunity and set up localized routing without node assistance.

Localized routing provides three key benefits:

Reduced transport network load: The path between an access gateway and the core network (where the LMA sits) is often the cost and performance bottleneck. Offloading traffic to the access network reduces this burden.

Lower latency: When two nodes are topologically close but their LMA is far away, direct paths significantly reduce delay and packet loss, especially for real-time applications.

Improved LMA scalability: The LMA represents a forwarding bottleneck for many MAGs. Localized routing reduces traffic through the LMA, allowing it to handle more mobile nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: It is slow, expensive, and hard on the main post office. A direct path between neighbors is faster, cheaper, and easier on the whole system.

sections.title: Use Cases and Topologies
sections.content:
This document focuses on communication between mobile nodes that are both registered with PMIPv6 LMAs within the same provider domain. It does not cover communication with correspondent nodes outside the PMIPv6 network.

Use cases are classified by the number of MAGs and LMAs involved:

A11: Both nodes attach to the same MAG and have the same LMA. The MAG can forward traffic directly between them. PMIPv6 base specs mention this but do not fully specify how to set it up.

A12: Both nodes attach to the same MAG but have different LMAs. The MAG can forward directly if both LMAs agree to allow it.

A21: Nodes attach to different MAGs but have the same LMA. The LMA coordinates setup of routing state on both MAGs so they can forward directly.

A22: Nodes attach to different MAGs and different LMAs. Both LMAs must coordinate the setup, which increases complexity and risk of race conditions during node handover.

The document also addresses roaming scenarios where mobile nodes move between provider domains, requiring consistent localized routing policies across domain boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Kids on the same street, same street with different postal branches, different streets same branch, or different streets and different branches. Each setup needs different coordination.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.content:
Before localized routing can work, the network infrastructure must:

Detect the possibility: By examining source and destination addresses of data packets, determine whether localized routing is feasible (both nodes in the same domain, for example).

Initiate a procedure: Trigger the setup of a localized routing path when the opportunity is detected.

Discover relevant entities: Find the LMA(s) and MAG(s) that maintain information about the mobile nodes and can provide routing addresses.

Control setup and maintenance: Manage the localized routing path during handover when nodes move to new gateways, and terminate the path when it is no longer needed.

Enforce policy: Operators may want to disallow localized routing for certain flows (for example, to ensure traffic traverses a charging function on the LMA). The solution must support policy-based authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: Notice the kids are neighbors, ask the post office for permission, find the right local branch, set up a direct route, keep it working when they move, and respect the post office's rules.

sections.title: IPv4 Considerations
sections.content:
PMIPv6 can support IPv4 mobile nodes and IPv4 communication. When localized routing is applied to IPv4 traffic, additional challenges arise:

Encapsulation compatibility: The MAG must wrap IPv4 packets for forwarding to another MAG. Both MAGs must support the same encapsulation method (a protocol detail the solution must negotiate or mandate).

Address space overlap: Private IPv4 address ranges can overlap between different networks. To uniquely identify two communicating nodes, the solution may need additional tagging mechanisms beyond source and destination addresses alone.

Transport network consistency: The transport network between LMA and MAG may be IPv6 or IPv4. Deployments typically enforce consistency (all IPv6 or all IPv4 for operational simplicity), and localized routing should align with this choice.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 addresses might collide (two kids with the same number in different postal systems), and the mail truck might use IPv6 or IPv4 roads, so the whole system must pick one consistently.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
The protocol solution must prevent unauthorized changes to routing paths. In particular, the control plane must prevent malicious network components from blocking or hijacking mobile node traffic.

Mobile IPv6's return routability test cannot be used in PMIPv6 because mobile nodes do not participate in signaling. Instead, solutions must rely on infrastructure-based authentication, such as IPsec, between PMIPv6 components that are in the same domain.

When PMIPv6 components are within the same provider domain, existing security associations from the base PMIPv6 spec can be reused to protect signaling between MAGs and LMAs.

Signaling between two MAGs (which may be from different vendors) requires protection mechanisms. The same applies for signaling between two LMAs. These protection means must be specified by the protocol solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Bad guys might try to reroute mail. Without the kids helping, the post office must prove everyone is honest before changing the route. They use secret codes and trust between offices.
